newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-FRAIL FRENCH DIVA BACK TO TRIUMPHANT BEST.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FRAIL FRENCH DIVA BACK TO TRIUMPHANT BEST.

text.p: For a few minutes on Thursday the smile was gone and France's Mary Pierce had that familiar haunted look in her eyes.

She was 5-1 up in the first set of her Australian Open semifinal against 12th seed Amanda Coetzer when the South African started to fight back. Coetzer broke her serve, held her own, broke her again and served to even up the score.
The chance for Pierce to repeat her greatest triumph was slipping away. Two years after being crowned champion at Melbourne Park, she was losing to her own lack of self-belief.
But where once she might have surrendered, Pierce clung on, hit back and left the court a 7-5 6-1 winner with a date in Saturday's final against Swiss Martina Hingis.
In a sport whose big names leave nothing to chance in their drive for points, prize money and sponsorship deals, Pierce has always been an outsider, unable to hide her human frailties.

The fact that she's a statuesque blonde, 1.80 metres tall and the closest thing tennis has to a Hollywood-style glamour girl has not always helped. "Daffy Diva" was how one Australian newspaper described her on Thursday.

Pierce had a past even before she started winning titles. Born in Canada to a French mother, she went to live in the United States but was spurned by the U.S. Tennis Association because of the behaviour of her father and coach, Jim. She decided to play under the French flag instead.

Her father was banned from the tour after erupting in the stands at the 1993 French Open, forcing the 18-year-old to strike out on her own. The following year she was a finalist at Roland Garros, quarter-finalist at the U.S. Open and then won in Melbourne in January 1995.
Then began the slide. At the French Open a few months later, where she was knocked out in the fourth round, the pressure was already getting to her. A pulled groin added to her problems.

In Melbourne last year she became the first defending champion in the Open era of tennis to lose before the quarter-finals. In Paris a few months later she was booed off court after a petulant display of time-wasting.
There followed a long break from the game during which time she rested, trained in a Paris gym and had physiotherapy on a weak shoulder. She did not touch a racquet for three months.

"Some days I wasn't enjoying it as much because I just started feeling a lot of pressure and a lot of expectations and, you know, I probably wasn't fulfilling (them)," Pierce said on Thursday, recalling what she called her "hard times".
"That's why the three months off were very positive and very good for me because I was able to take a step back and to relax and just to enjoy really what I do."
Now her outlook has changed: "I've just been having fun, I've just been enjoying it ... I feel like my game is getting better and better with every match."
On centre court on Saturday against the world's top-ranked teenager, Pierce will be hoping to exorcise the last of her demons and put her tennis career back on course.
Win or lose, she'll remain one of the more intriguing figures in the world of tennis. It would take more than a simple grand slam title to change France's Daffy Diva.
